newsitem.title: DENMARK: SOCCER-EUROPEAN COACHES SEEK MORE TIME WITH PLAYERS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-EUROPEAN COACHES SEEK MORE TIME WITH PLAYERS.

text.p: European national coaches, concerned that big clubs are growing more powerful, have called for more time with their players so they can maintain their teams' standards.

"They fear international football could become watered down," UEFA technical director Andy Roxburgh said after the close of the European soccer body's three-day National Coaches convention on Wednesday.
Former Scotland manager Roxburgh said Berti Vogts, coach of Euro 96 winners Germany, had been at the forefront of the demands.
"Berti led the way with an impassioned plea for the protection of national teams," he said.

National coaches, holding their second convention since the inaugural Stockholm meeting two years ago after the 1994 World Cup, see Europe's major clubs becoming more powerful since the Bosman ruling removed restrictions on foreign players.

They say international football is now even more important because clubs are losing their national identity with polyglot squads and in order to work better with their players they need more time and new arrangements.
"The coaches are a bit concerned that in the post-Bosman era we're in the past," Roxburgh said. "In 1967, when Glasgow Celtic won the European Cup, all the players were local."
Roxburgh said UEFA's technical committee, of which Vogts is a new member, would meet in Amsterdam in November to discuss proposals put forward at the convention and then submit them to the executive.
The most important proposal was that rather than hold international matches in midweek, a few weekends per season should be put aside, allowing national teams to play twice in the space of 10 days.
The national coaches argue that this would also suit the clubs, because countries would need fewer periods in the season to play internationals.

In five 10-day periods countries could play 10 internationals and clubs in the domestic top divisions, which already take a weekend break ahead of a midweek international, would be asked to release players from a Monday to the Wednesday of the following week but less often in the season.
The idea was put forward about a year ago by veteran Danish international Michael Laudrup.
Roxburgh said the short spells national team coaches had with their squads was their biggest headache, especially since they rarely had players around after a match except during a tournament.

Denmark's new national team coach Bo Johansson, successor to 1992 European championship winner Richard Moeller Nielsen, said: "It would be super to have the players after a game. It would also give us more of a chance with team-building which was also a topic of great importance dealt with here."
Vogts gave the convention an insight into his preparations, particularly the psychological aspect, for his Euro 96 success.
"We tend to think of the Germans as just very hard working," Johansson said. "It was nice to discover they are much more than just hard work."

The coaches discussed the sudden death "golden goal", with most of them expressing their dislike of it, the need to clarify the offside rule in terms of whether or not a player on the fringe of the action was influencing play, and yellow cards.
A grading system was proposed to differentiate between violent play and dissent. "Should a player be suspended for talking too much," Roxburgh said.
They agreed there should be more cooperation with referees to try to resolve problems like some big refereeing mistakes during the Euro 96 tournament in England in June.

Former France coach Gerard Houllier, also on the technical committee, said the coaches had been much more positive about the second convention despite Vogts' initial fear he was wasting his time coming to Copenhagen and were keen to repeat it.
